channel.title: Star Stuff — Changelog
channel.description: Why the Star Stuff collection changed, newest first — pieces added, pieces substantially revised, and every fact-check and attribution audit, including corrections to our own errors. The companion feed to What's New, which carries the pieces themselves.
channel.copyright: CC BY-SA 4.0 · Stimpunks Foundation × More Realms

item.title: Glimmer Wire, edition five: five papers read end to end, and six stories held over a single word
item.description:
2026 · September 25

The weekly scan behind Glimmers, at its own page. Seven filed, six held, three seeds. Median lag 85 days, range 2 to 157.

  • New — Seven filed — three verified, one contested, three plausible
  • Fact-check — Six held, five of them over a word the paper does not use
  • Site — What refused, and one refusal that returned a valid page

item.title: The changelog has a feed of its own now, because “what came out” and “what we got wrong” are not one subscription
item.description:
2026 · September 21

A second RSS feed at changelog.xml, generated from the monthly archive pages by the tool that already reads them. Ryan’s call, 21 September 2026.

  • Site — A separate feed, not a merged one

item.title: The feed was dating every entry by whoever generated it last, and told a different day than the page it came from
item.description:
2026 · September 20

A generator bug that only exists once a project has two people in two places. Found by a diff that rewrote all 102 dates in feed.xml and changed nothing else.

  • Site — A generator may not read the machine it runs on — not the clock, not the timezone

item.title: We spent five weeks asking permission for a character we own, and the error survived because it looked like care
item.description:
2026 · September 20

A correction to The Quillery and the Easter Eggs collection card. Esmx the Porkypine was commissioned by the Stimpunks Foundation, who hold the rights; three sentences on this site said otherwise, and one of them said it inside a ledger row that recorded the commission two clauses later.

  • Fact-check — “Not ours to redraw stroke for stroke” — wrong about who holds the rights, and published for five weeks

item.title: Glimmer Wire, edition four — four papers read end to end, and a median lag that tripled because of it
item.description:
2026 · September 18

Eight items filed, six held, four verified. The best reading week this scan has had, and the lag axis went the wrong way as a direct result — which is worth more than a flattering number and is explained on the page rather than smoothed.

  • New — Glimmer Wire — edition of 18 September 2026
  • Fact-check — Six held, two of them papers we wanted — and three sentences of our own cut before publishing

item.title: The Big Bang had no location, so it happened where you are sitting — and a geometry with no middle has no far end
item.description:
2026 · September 17

Zine No. 111. Prompted by a Brian Cox episode and then built entirely from the papers, because the transcript turned out to be unusable. Two errors on one spread were caught before shipping, one of them by a reader, and both are recorded below rather than quietly fixed.

  • New — It Happened Where You Are Sitting — Zine No. 111
  • Fact-check — Two errors on one spread, caught before shipping: a curvature sign that made the page contradict itself, and a dataset label that hid the mechanism

item.title: This page had grown to 1.4 megabytes, so it is now one page per month — and every old link still lands on the right entry
item.description:
2026 · September 14

The changelog was a single page carrying every dated entry since the collection started. It was 449 KB to download just to read the newest one, and growing by about six entries a day. Split by month, with an index at the address it always had.

  • Site — A running log on one page gets worse every week, not better

item.title: A second table of contents that lives in the margin, and gets out of the way when the page gets wide
item.description:
2026 · September 14

A row of small ticks down the left margin that becomes the contents list when you point at it, ending in a shooting star. On the 34 pages that have a contents list, and only where there is room for it — which on some pages changes as you scroll.

  • Site — The rail, and the four things that were wrong with it first

item.title: Eight of our seventeen collection pages were telling machines they held a fraction of what they hold
item.description:
2026 · September 14

Yesterday’s pass found one page whose structured data carried another page’s title. Writing a check for it turned up something larger: the machine-readable table of contents on most of the collection pages had been drifting from the actual shelf for months.

  • Site — A check for structured data that describes the wrong page

item.title: The sentence this whole collection is named after was being sung to audiences three years before Carl Sagan published it
item.description:
2026 · September 14

The oldest rack here was the only one of the eight with no essay in front of it. It has one now, and the argument is a chronology that puts us last rather than first. Plus: fifty-four section labels across the Sound collection that were never headings at all, and two pieces of structured data quietly describing the wrong page.

  • Revised — L★S Playlist — an essay on the order it actually happened in
  • Site — Fifty-four section labels that looked like headings and were not
  • Fact-check — Two pieces of structured data describing the wrong page

item.title: Our design page said this site depends on Google’s font servers. Our privacy page said it doesn’t. The privacy page was right.
item.description:
2026 · September 13

A sentence that stopped being true on 9 September and stayed up for four days, plus four more places carrying the same dead claim — two of them as instructions telling the next person to put the dependency back.

  • Fact-check — Two pages on one site disagreeing about whether it phones Google

item.title: Twenty-four long essays here had no table of contents, and eight of them run past five thousand words
item.description:
2026 · September 13

A reader arriving from a search result landed in the middle of a document with no way to see its shape. One page on the site had a contents list; it has been made into a house component and given to every essay that earns one.

  • Site — A map at the top of every essay, and two pages whose headings could not be linked to at all

item.title: The tool that writes our security policy could be fooled by a sentence about itself, and the reason was a Turkish letter
item.description:
2026 · September 13

Logged a few hours ago as a known weakness we had failed twice to repair. It is repaired now, and the cause turned out to be something this site had already written down in its own search code.

  • Site — A scan that read prose as markup, and a lowercase that moved every index after it

item.title: You can now change the words on a page without editing HTML — and there is a list of what it will not let you change
item.description:
2026 · September 13

A bookmark that makes a page editable and copies out a patch for somebody to apply. It cannot save, nothing on the site loads it, and the most important part of it is the list of things it refuses to touch.

  • Site — An editor that cannot save, and will not touch a quotation

item.title: A style rule kept for a class no page has ever used
item.description:
2026 · September 13

The smallest item on the housekeeping list, finished for completeness: one selector in the shared stylesheet, waiting since it was written for markup that never arrived.

  • Site — The last dead selector in the shared stylesheet

item.title: Twenty-four style rules that were written out a thousand times, and two wrong theories about why that was safe
item.description:
2026 · September 13

A colophon heading, a page counter, a byline: the same rules, copied into page after page. They now live in one place. Getting there took three attempts, because the first two moved rules that looked identical and were not interchangeable.

  • Site — 1,015 copies of 24 rules become 24 rules
  • Fact-check — Two wrong theories, both caught by rendering all 207 pages

item.title: One page-turning function instead of 107, and the security policy got a quarter smaller for free
item.description:
2026 · September 13

Every paged zine carried its own copy of the code that turns the page — 107 copies in 17 slightly different versions. The only thing that varied between them was the number of spreads, which the shared file could already count. All 107 now share one implementation.

  • Site — 115,101 bytes of duplicated page-turning code, replaced by 88 lines
  • Site — Duplicated script is duplicated security surface
  • Fact-check — Tested by driving all 107, and then again with the real policy switched on

item.title: A thousand style rules that styled nothing, and the two bugs in the tool that found them
item.description:
2026 · September 13

Every page carries its own stylesheet, copied forward from the page before it. Over 110 zines that accumulated 1,054 rules aimed at things none of those pages contain. They are gone, and nothing on the site looks different — which is the entire claim, and it was measured rather than assumed.

  • Site — 1,054 dead selectors removed from 119 pages
  • Fact-check — The tool was wrong twice before it was right, and one of the errors would have broken every zine
  • Site — The audit is kept, and deliberately not made a gate

item.title: We said the cover artwork lay across the subtitle on 93 covers. It was 23, and we made the exact mistake our own checker was built to avoid
item.description:
2026 · September 13

Yesterday’s cover-collision entry carried four numbers measured the wrong way. The headline finding stands; three of the four figures under it do not. Found while Ryan asked an unrelated question about one zine’s stylesheet.

  • Correction — A drawing’s box is not a drawing
  • Site — One zine had a breakpoint tuned for a table it never had

item.title: A byline has one field and contribution has fourteen — the constructive half of the credit run
item.description:
2026 · September 12

Zine No. 110 joins Star Stuff, which now holds forty-three. It is the practice piece: not who was wronged, but what the format underneath all of it can and cannot record, and what to do instead at any scale.

  • New — Fourteen Kinds of Doing — Zine No. 110, 12 spreads
  • Fact-check — A paper we could not read, and a figure two sources disagree about
  • Fact-check — Update, same day: we got the paper, and it was better than our hedge
  • Revised — What the zine says about this site, which is not flattering

item.title: A catalogue of missing names, including the two stories we had to correct against ourselves
item.description:
2026 · September 12

Field Guide No. 25 joins Field Guides, which now holds twenty-four. It sorts eleven pieces of work not by how famous the person was but by how the name came off — and two of its entries exist to correct the popular telling in the direction that costs the argument something.

  • New — A Field Guide to Missing Names — Field Guide No. 25, 11 entries
  • Fact-check — Two entries that correct the story against our own argument
  • Revised — Field Guides — counts re-derived, and a stale figure in our own notes

item.title: 105 of our 108 zine covers were broken on a phone, and the gate that would have caught it had written down in advance that it would not
item.description:
2026 · September 12

Found while building No. 109. On a 375px screen the ghosted issue number printed through the issue line or the title on 103 pages, and the cover artwork lay across the words on every cover that has any. It had been like that since the first cover in July. Fixed in one shared rule; the checker now measures two screen widths instead of one.

  • Site — Cover ornaments now flow on a phone instead of being pinned to a corner that is not there
  • Site — The collision checker had said, in its own file, exactly what it was going to miss
  • Fact-check — The first phone run reported 256 problems that were not problems, on twelve of our own pages

item.title: The primary source contradicted the zine we set out to write, so we wrote the one it supports
item.description:
2026 · September 12

Zine No. 109 joins Young Readers, which now holds fourteen. It is a read-aloud about who gets named — and two things it was going to say were cut, both because the discoverer’s own account says otherwise.

  • New — A Bit of Scruff — Zine No. 109, read-aloud, ages 4–8
  • Fact-check — Two things we were going to print, cut against the primary
  • Revised — Young Readers — a count that stopped adding up two zines ago

item.title: Four letters, and the half of the 1953 paper nobody quotes — plus the finding that prompted this zine and is not in it
item.description:
2026 · September 12

Zine No. 105 joins Young Readers, which now holds eleven. It is a read-aloud about the genetic alphabet, a subject this site had never touched: before this week no page here contained base pair, adenine, guanine or genetic alphabet.

  • New — The Same Four Letters — Zine No. 105, read-aloud, ages 4–8
  • Fact-check — The finding that prompted this zine is deliberately absent from it — on our own wire’s advice

item.title: The man who coined the genetic code wrote the correction four lines later. It took the rest of us eighty years
item.description:
2026 · September 12 · latest

Zine No. 108 joins How We Got Here as its seventeenth chain: twelve links, nine documented, two contested, one leap. It is the adult companion to yesterday’s read-aloud, and it goes all the way to 2025.

  • New — Too Narrow — Zine No. 108, a chain in twelve links
  • Fact-check — One leap, marked and then declined — and a joint graded contested because we could not source it

item.title: An onion has five times more DNA than you do, so whatever it is, it is not a plan of anybody
item.description:
2026 · September 12

Zine No. 107 joins Young Readers, which now holds thirteen, and closes a three-part arc: No. 105 gave the alphabet, No. 106 the code that reads it, and this one asks what the whole thing is. It exists to pay a debt — No. 106 cited a paper as a lead it had not read, and this zine read it.

  • New — The Onion Has More Than You — Zine No. 107, read-aloud, ages 4–8
  • Fact-check — A lead we published as unread, now read — and what the zine declines to do with it

item.title: We said a 1961 paper could not be read. It could, and our own working notes already said how
item.description:
2026 · September 12

Zine No. 106 shipped this morning saying that Nirenberg and Matthaei’s 1961 paper — the experiment that read the very first codon — was held only as scanned page images, and that a spread on it had been cut for that reason. The paper is readable. The claim has been corrected on the zine and here.

  • Fact-check — One blocked route is not unreachable

item.title: One number was doing two jobs, so it came apart three times — twice at our own hands
item.description:
2026 · September 12

The Young Readers page has a line saying how many of its pieces hand the child something to do. It has been wrong, in one direction or another, since before either of this week’s zines. The figure is now eight of the twelve, and the eight are named on the page so it cannot drift again.

  • Fact-check — “Something to do” and “a demonstration” are different sets, and one number was counting both

item.title: Sixty-four words, twenty beads — and the promise No. 105 made on its own face, kept
item.description:
2026 · September 12

Zine No. 106 joins Young Readers, which now holds twelve. Yesterday’s zine said in its grown-up layer that the genetic code “is not in this zine at all.” This is that promise being kept, and it goes somewhere the first one could not.

  • New — More Than One Way to Spell It — Zine No. 106, read-aloud, ages 4–8
  • Fact-check — Nothing written from memory, two papers declared unread, and a famous result kept with its criticism attached

item.title: We said no page here contacts Google for fonts. One still did, and it was the one no sweep could reach
item.description:
2026 · September 12

On 9 September the four typeface families were self-hosted and every font <link> and preconnect was removed site-wide. Our privacy page has said so since. It was true of 200 pages and false of one.

  • Fact-check — whats-new.html carried two preconnects and a Google Fonts stylesheet for three days

item.title: A read-aloud about the Goldilocks Zone — and a correction, from the reader who proposed it, that made the zine better
item.description:
2026 · September 11

Zine No. 104 joins Young Readers, which now holds ten. The fairy tale says one bowl is right and two are wrong. The science that borrowed its nickname says nearly the opposite, and this piece follows that until it arrives somewhere the collection has never been.

  • New — Just Right For Whom? — Zine No. 104, read-aloud, ages 4–8
  • Fact-check — The premise the zine was proposed on was half wrong — and then our correction to it was wrong too

item.title: Queering Earth introduces itself by naming this site. The front page now names it back
item.description:
2026 · September 11

There is a sibling site, built by the same two organizations, working the half of the shelf this one does not. Its front page has been pointing here since it opened on 7 September; ours pointed nowhere. A reader who arrived at this end had no way of knowing the other end existed.

  • Site — A second paragraph on the front page, and the difference between the two sites stated rather than smoothed

item.title: Glimmer Wire, edition three — the week the network answered, and a correction of ours still out on the wire
item.description:
2026 · September 11

The third weekly edition of Glimmer Wire. Seven items filed, five held, and for the first time three papers read end to end rather than at one remove. Also the longest lag the page has measured, and a held item that is not a story we found thin — it is a figure this page corrected last week, still travelling unchanged.

  • Working paper — Seven filed: a Jurassic chorus, a species that is several, a cat that was never a cheetah
  • Held — A figure we corrected last week is still on the wire, and a 2022 paper arrived as a discovery

item.title: Yes, you may train on this — said out loud, to thirteen named crawlers
item.description:
2026 · September 10

We have never stated a position on AI crawlers, which meant the answer was whatever a wildcard happened to imply. It is now written down, per agent, with the reasoning on the file's own face. Also: a page had been offering search engines nothing at all for four days, and nothing here could see it.

  • Site — The decision, and the argument we did not take
  • Correction — Three crawler names in our reference were out of date, and one of our pages was invisible to search engines
  • Site — A page for agents about how to read us without getting it wrong

item.title: Ctrl+F now reaches the field notes while they are still folded away — and the thing we said needed fixing did not
item.description:
2026 · September 10

Twenty-four field guides keep their notes collapsed behind a click, and those notes are the guide. Search the page for a remembered phrase and the browser now finds it inside a closed card, opens it, and scrolls to it. Separately: we had named the wrong thing as broken, and checked before changing it.

  • Correction — We said the front page's card descriptions were unfindable. They were not
  • Site — What was actually unreachable: the field notes
  • Site — The trap: making text hidden a different way breaks four things that reveal it
  • Site — The zines are not done, and it is a question about reading rather than a checkbox

item.title: A favicon that only worked in one place, and two link relations we said were standard and are not
item.description:
2026 · September 10

Small, overdue plumbing: real icons for phones and old browsers, a manifest so the site installs properly, and a machine-readable index of everything on this origin that a program can read. The interesting part is what fell out of checking our own claims against a registry.

  • Correction — Two of the five link relations we send on every response are not registered
  • Site — The favicon worked in a tab and nowhere else
  • Site — It installs, and deliberately keeps the way out
  • Site — One address that lists everything here a program can read

item.title: If you replace our colours with your own, 4,862 diagram labels had almost no contrast — and the first thing we “found” was not real
item.description:
2026 · September 10

Some readers override every site's colours with a small high-contrast palette of their own. We had not one rule for that, from the first page in July until today. Nobody reported this. We went looking because a specification asked a question we had never asked ourselves — and then spent most of the day fixing something that was never broken, which is the part of this worth reading.

  • Site — The diagrams were never wrong. The ground moved out from under them
  • Correction — We reported 229 invisible headings, including our own wordmark. There were none
  • Site — Twenty-four labels are exempt, and recolouring them is what would have broken them
  • Site — A ninth gate, and the reason to trust it is that it failed first

item.title: We said our sister site ships Markdown mirrors with no staleness check. It does not, and we should have looked at the gate rather than the comment
item.description:
2026 · September 9

The entry below this one says Queering Earth's Markdown generator has no check behind it, so an edited page would ship a stale copy unnoticed. That is false. Its check-metadata.mjs catches exactly that, and catches a missing discovery link too. Both verified firing today. The correction matters more than most because it was a public claim that somebody else's work was deficient.

  • Correction — What we said, what is true, and how we got it wrong

item.title: Fifty-seven pages now have a Markdown twin at the same address — and a hundred and forty-one deliberately do not
item.description:
2026 · September 9

Add .md to the address of an essay, a collection page or this changelog and you get the same words as Markdown, derived from the page itself. The zines, field guides and print sheets are left out on purpose, and the reason is the more interesting half.

  • Site — Why three-quarters of the site has no Markdown copy
  • Site — Ported from Queering Earth, with the gate it was missing
  • Correction — The fifth time in one day that a tool mistook prose for the thing it describes

item.title: A tool called build-whats-new was building four things, only one of which is What’s New
item.description:
2026 · September 9

Renamed to build-derived.mjs. It generates What’s New, the feed, llms.txt and the security.txt, and the old name described a quarter of it.

  • Site — Why a name mattered enough to change

item.title: Two hundred and thirty-three onclick attributes are gone, and with them the one weak keyword in the security policy
item.description:
2026 · September 9

The policy shipped an hour ago needed 'unsafe-hashes' to permit six strings — the handlers on every pager button, every print sheet and the search form. Those buttons are now bound in JavaScript, there are zero inline event handlers left on the site, and the keyword removed itself.

  • Site — The pager still pages, which was the whole risk
  • Correction — Our own tool counted a comment as a live handler
  • Audit — And the test could not tell “broken” from “not applicable”

item.title: This morning we said a real Content-Security-Policy was impossible here. It is not — we had stopped at two options when there are three
item.description:
2026 · September 9

A full CSP now ships on every response. An inline script injected into any page on this site does not run, and that is checked by injecting one into a browser rather than asserted. The reasoning we published earlier today was sound in both its halves and wrong in its conclusion, which is a nicer way to be wrong than usual and still worth naming.

  • Correction — “A real policy needs nonces or unsafe-inline” — both true, and it missed hashes
  • Site — What the policy actually forbids now
  • Site — Generated, gated, and tested against the site working

item.title: If you find a hole in this site, there is now somewhere to send it that isn't a public issue
item.description:
2026 · September 9

A security policy and an RFC 9116 security.txt, pointing at a private reporting channel that had to be switched on before it existed. The interesting part is the Expires field, which is a file that goes invalid on a date and says nothing about it — so it is gated rather than diarised.

  • Site — A private channel, because an issue on a public repository is a disclosure
  • Site — A file that expires, on a site with a documented weakness for things that go stale

item.title: A description on this site read “The culture end of Star Stuff, where” and stopped — for a month, because of one unescaped quotation mark
item.description:
2026 · September 9

The site now publishes an index for language models, generated from the same collection cards every other list here comes from. Writing it meant reading all seventeen collection descriptions, which is how we found five meta tags on three pages silently cut in half by an unescaped quote — and that fault has earned check-markup.mjs a ninth check.

  • Correction — Five descriptions were truncated in every browser, and the source looked fine
  • Site — A ninth check, so that cannot happen quietly again
  • Site — llms.txt — curated, which is the hard part

item.title: One picture on this site weighed 2.3 megabytes to be displayed four hundred pixels wide
item.description:
2026 · September 9

The images are now AVIF with WebP and JPEG behind them, and sized to what the page actually draws rather than to whatever the original happened to be. A modern browser now fetches 600 KB of images where it used to fetch 4,216 KB — 86% less. Also: the last three pages with a skipped heading level are fixed, and a separate check of every tap target on the site came back clean.

  • Site — AVIF, WebP, JPEG — and sizes taken from measurement rather than from the CSS
  • Site — What the smaller files cost, stated rather than buried
  • Site — Three pages skipped a heading level; a tag change with the selector to match
  • Audit — Every tap target on the site, measured — and the measurement was wrong twice first

item.title: Every page on this site handed your address to Google before it drew a word — and we only found out because we sat down to write the privacy page
item.description:
2026 · September 9

The site now has a privacy statement, and writing it changed the site first. Four typeface families are self-hosted as of today, which ends the only third-party request a plain page here was making. On the way we found that eight pages were rendering a fallback typeface, and that this morning's own changelog entry overstated what youtube-nocookie actually promises. Both below.

  • Site — The fonts came off Google, because the honest sentence was unwriteable
  • Correction — We called the youtube-nocookie move a privacy win. It is one, and narrower than we implied
  • Site — Eight pages were rendering a typeface they never asked for
  • Site — The privacy page, and a link to it on all 198 pages

item.title: A screen reader can now tell you which column a table cell is in — and two numbers we published this morning were wrong
item.description:
2026 · September 9

The second half of the accessibility audit: 199 header cells given a scope, four tables that had no accessible name at all given a caption, and 161 table names that read “the The…” repaired. Corrected below: both table figures in this morning's entry were overstated, one of them because our own counting method was broken.

  • Correction — We said 282 of 299 header cells and 28 uncaptioned tables. Both numbers were wrong
  • Site — 199 header cells given a scope, so a cell knows which column it belongs to
  • Site — 161 table names read “How a default reading misreads the The Biggest Mouth in the Sea”
  • Site — Four tables that had no name at all, and a caption that must not contain units

item.title: Every page on this site made a keyboard reader walk past six links to reach the first word — on all 197 of them, since the first one shipped
item.description:
2026 · September 9

An audit of starstuff.earth against The Website Specification, and the fixes it earned. The largest was a skip link, which we did not have anywhere. Also: 66 YouTube embeds moved to the no-cookie host, four security response headers, a real 404 page instead of the host’s default, and intrinsic dimensions on every image. Two faults were found while fixing, and both are logged below.

  • Site — A skip link, on all 197 pages
  • Site — 66 YouTube embeds were still on the cookie-setting host
  • Site — A 404 page that offers a way back
  • Site — Four security headers, and honest limits on a fifth
  • Site — Two faults found while fixing, neither of them the thing being fixed
  • Site — Intrinsic dimensions on every image, and what is still outstanding

item.title: The blood a horned lizard squirts at a coyote is made out of the ants it eats — and the viral claim we went looking to confirm is in none of the ten papers
item.description:
2026 · September 8

Zine No. 103, the eighth Kin piece. Commissioned to check a claim, and the check came back negative — so the zine is the animal, and the claim gets graded on two of its fourteen spreads. Three sources are named on the page as unread rather than paraphrased, including the video itself. Corrected the same day: the zine said the schoolyard children had done something now illegal. They had not — they only looked.

  • New piece — The Blood Was Made of Ants — Zine No. 103
  • Claim graded — “Fire ants are vanishing across Texas — scientists finally found what’s hunting them”
  • Declared unread — Three sources named as gaps on the page, including the video
  • Refused as evidence — A genus-level hit that would have read as a finding
  • Correction — We said looking at a horned lizard is illegal. It is not, and the source lists what is
  • Fixed before shipping — A cover motif redrawn, and nine diagram grounds that would have printed as slabs of ink

item.title: A leaf does not fade. It stays green, and green, and green — and then it turns in about a week
item.description:
2026 · September 7

Zine No. 102, the ninth Young Readers piece. The frame this zine was proposed on did not survive its own sources, and the correction is now a spread of its own rather than a quiet substitution. A count on the collection page was corrected rather than incremented.

  • New piece — It Stays Green, and Then It Goes — Zine No. 102
  • Corrected before shipping — The tidy sentence we proposed the zine on is tidier than the measurements
  • Correction — A count we incremented instead of deriving, on our own collection page
  • Fixed before shipping — The cover art ran under the issue number again
